title: Library of Alexandria burns: AI companies are destroying books in bulk
excerpt: The artificial intelligence industry, having already stripped the open web of its bark and devoured every morsel of its illegally acquired…
content_html:
The artificial intelligence industry, having already stripped the open web of its bark and devoured every morsel of its illegally acquired libraries, has developed a new appetite. Millions of physical books are now being bought in bulk and fed into a process that the industry nervously calls “destructive scanning”.

Data acquisition increasingly involves cutting the spines from millions of books, scanning them and then shredding and discarding them afterward.

The service comes courtesy of a company called ISBNdb. They promise to obtain “up to one million titles per order.” They specifically tout “older, rare and specialist volumes” as premium training data because books from the pre-2022 era are “structurally guaranteed” to be free of AI contamination. As AI starts to feed on itself into a delirious loop, information from the old world becomes more valuable to the momentum and continuation of large language models.

Read more about AI and the arts from Derek McArthur:

  • A prestigious literary competition is being accused of rewarding AI-written works
  • Replace all artists? The strange logic of the AI art defenders
  • A rapper is pretending his new viral hit isn't a blatant AI creation
  • OpenAI’s Sora was going to destroy Hollywood... until it came abruptly crashing down
  • Can we pass a law banning the sale of Highland cow AI art?
  • A nonsensical AI-generated mural is the last thing Glasgow ever needs
  • This film veteran was stunned when he asked AI to give him ideas

The company's marketing material is blunt about the reality of what happens to the books. "'AI company destroys two million books' is not a headline that generates sympathy," its website states. It offers non-disclosure agreements to buyers and advises them to frame the work as "digital preservation".

We are talking about books that have survived through the many scourges of history and have become rare due to their life as an obscurity before the information age.

Small booksellers across Europe and the United States have noticed a sudden surge in bulk orders for rare and out-of-print titles. One bookseller told 404 Media that he went from selling about 20 books a week to hundreds, including hard-to-find foreign language works. "It benefits me financially as well as by clearing out old inventory that is otherwise unlikely to sell," he said. "On the other hand, I don't like the end-use, and I don't like that uncommon books are being pulped."

Okay, and on the other hand, these things cannot be replaced. Once a final non-digitised copy of a book is shredded, it’s gone forever. And the version that is digitised becomes at the mercy of AI interpretation rather than a straight, accurate representation of the work.

A collection of rare books and manuscripts at Oxford University (Image: Getty)

Anthropic, the company behind the chatbot Claude, has been a major driver of this practice. Internal documents made public during a copyright lawsuit revealed a program called “Project Panama” launched in 2024. Court filings described an industrial-scale operation using a "hydraulic powered cutting machine" to slice the spines off millions of books, which were then fed through "high speed, high quality, production level scanners". An internal memo called it "our effort to disruptively scan all the world's books" and noted, "we do not want it to be known that we are pursuing this project." Anthropic hired the former head of Google Books specifically to help acquire what the company described as "all the books in the world".

The legal framework enabling this comes from a federal judge's ruling in the Anthropic copyright case. The court determined that by making a digital copy and destroying the physical original in a one-for-one transfer, the process qualifies as "transformative" and falls under fair use protections. The reasoning is that since only one copy exists at a time, it's not traditional piracy. This ruling sets a precedent that allows the practice to wildly accelerate.

Read more from Derek McArthur:

  • Does the Mack need to be faithfully rebuilt or are we just scared of our own future?
  • Movie studios are circling like sharks to buy the biggest online review platform
  • This year’s Cannes came and went. Is cinema in danger of becoming a niche hobby?
  • Swapping the boss won't put back together a broken Creative Scotland

Rare booksellers across multiple countries are now receiving similar suspicious purchase requests. In the Netherlands, an antiquarian bookseller received an email from a Singapore-based company claiming to be working on "a new project focused on collecting books in multiple languages". The attached list contained 3,000 English-language titles organized by ISBN number, ranging from folklore and fairytales to technical manuals and science texts. Similar reports have emerged from Switzerland, Spain, and Germany. The booksellers involved concluded the books were destined for AI training because no collector or reseller would need such a random assortment of obscure titles.

So who will be the knight in shining armour and stop such a senseless and wasteful practice? Elon Musk stated on his social media platform X that he instructed his own AI team "to preserve any rare books in a library and scan them the hard way vs just cutting off the spine and scanning". Thanks for that, Elon, but it’s hard to take the moral right of someone seriously when their own AI model generated child sexual abuse material.

Destroying books is very efficient for AI companies and, according to the courts, legal. But the cost is a permanent loss that carries historical and cultural significance beyond words printed on the page. The books that survive this process will live the rest of days as mindless data points in a model, their physical forms long turned to pulp. Unless the legal framework changes or public pressure forces companies to preserve the originals, the Library of Alexandria will burn yet again.

Derek McArthur is an artist and arts writer specialising in cinema and culture. He writes a weekly arts column for The Herald.

But the cost is a permanent loss that carries historical and cultural significance beyond words printed on the page. The books that survive this process will live the rest of days as mindless data points in a model, their physical forms long turned to pulp. Unless the legal framework changes or public pressure forces companies to preserve the originals, the Library of Alexandria will burn yet again.

content_html_zh:
人工智能产业已经剥去了开放网络的外皮，吞噬了非法获取的图书馆的每一部分，现在已经产生了新的胃口。 现在，数以百万计的实体书被批量购买，并被送入业界紧张地称之为“破坏性扫描”的过程中。

数据采集​​越来越多地涉及从数百万本书中切割书脊、扫描它们，然后将它们撕碎并丢弃。

该服务由一家名为 ISBNdb 的公司提供。 他们承诺“每个订单最多可获得 100 万部图书”。 他们特别将“较旧的、稀有的和专业的书籍”吹捧为优质培训数据，因为 2022 年之前的书籍“在结构上保证”不会受到人工智能污染。 随着人工智能开始陷入疯狂的循环，来自旧世界的信息对于大型语言模型的动力和延续变得更有价值。

阅读德里克·麦克阿瑟 (Derek McArthur) 撰写的有关人工智能和艺术的更多内容：

  • 一项著名的文学竞赛被指控奖励人工智能撰写的作品
  • 替换所有艺人？ AI艺术捍卫者的奇怪逻辑
  • 一名说唱歌手假装他的新热门歌曲不是公然的人工智能创作
  • OpenAI 的 Sora 想要摧毁好莱坞…… 直到它突然崩溃
  • 我们可以通过一项法律禁止销售高地奶牛人工智能艺术品吗？
  • 人工智能生成的荒谬壁画是格拉斯哥最不需要的东西
  • 当这位电影老手向人工智能请教时，他惊呆了

该公司的营销材料直言不讳地讲述了书籍所发生的真实情况。 其网站称：“‘人工智能公司销毁了 200 万本书’这个标题不会引起同情。” 它向买家提供保密协议，并建议他们将作品设计为“数字保存”。

我们谈论的是那些在历史的许多灾难中幸存下来的书籍，并且由于它们在信息时代之前默默无闻而变得稀有。

欧洲和美国的小书商注意到稀有和绝版图书的批量订单突然激增。 一位书商告诉 404 Media，他的销量从每周约 20 本书增加到数百本书，其中包括很难找到的外文作品。 他说：“这不仅对我有经济上的好处，还能清理掉那些不太可能卖掉的旧库存。” “另一方面，我不喜欢最终用途，也不喜欢不常见的书籍被制成纸浆。”

好吧，另一方面，这些东西是无法替代的。 一旦一本书的最终非数字化副本被粉碎，它就永远消失了。 数字化的版本受到人工智能解释的支配，而不是作品的直接、准确的表达。

牛津大学珍本和手稿收藏（图片来源：Getty）

聊天机器人 Claude 背后的公司 Anthropic 一直是这种做法的主要推动者。 在版权诉讼期间公开的内部文件显示，一个名为“巴拿马计划”的计划于 2024 年启动。 法庭文件描述了一项工业规模的操作，使用“液压动力切割机”将数百万本书的书脊切下来，然后将其输入“高速、高质量、生产水平的扫描仪”。 一份内部备忘录称其为“我们破坏性地扫描世界上所有书籍的努力”，并指出，“我们不希望人们知道我们正在开展这个项目。” Anthropic 专门聘请了谷歌图书的前负责人来帮助收购该公司所说的“世界上所有的图书”。

实现这一点的法律框架来自联邦法官对人类版权案的裁决。 法院认定，通过制作数字副本并以一对一的方式销毁物理原件，该过程符合“变革性”并受到合理使用保护。 原因是，由于一次仅存在一份副本，因此这不是传统的盗版。 这一裁决开创了先例，使得这种做法得以大幅加速。

阅读德里克·麦克阿瑟的更多内容：

  • 麦克是否需要忠实地重建，还是我们只是害怕自己的未来？
  • 电影制片厂像鲨鱼一样盘旋收购最大的在线评论平台
  • 今年的戛纳来了又去了。 电影是否有成为小众爱好的危险？
  • 更换老板不会让支离破碎的创意苏格兰重新组合起来

多个国家的稀有书商现在都收到类似的可疑购买请求。 在荷兰，一位古籍书商收到了一家新加坡公司发来的电子邮件，声称正在开展“一个专注于收集多种语言书籍的新项目”。 所附清单包含 3,000 种英文书籍，按 ISBN 编号排列，范围从民间传说和童话故事到技术手册和科学文本。 瑞士、西班牙和德国也出现了类似的报告。 相关书商得出的结论是，这些书注定要接受人工智能培训，因为没有收藏家或经销商需要如此随机分类的晦涩标题。

那么谁会成为身披闪亮盔甲的骑士，阻止这种毫无意义和浪费的做法呢？ 埃隆·马斯克在他的社交媒体平台 X 上表示，他指示自己的人工智能团队“保存图书馆中的所有珍本书籍，并以艰难的方式扫描它们，而不是仅仅切断书脊并扫描”。 谢谢你，埃隆，但是当某人自己的人工智能模型生成儿童性虐待材料时，很难认真对待某人的道德权利。

对于人工智能公司来说，销毁书籍非常有效，而且根据法院的说法，这是合法的。 但代价是永久性的损失，其历史和文化意义超出了页面上印刷的文字。 在这个过程中幸存下来的书籍将在余下的日子里作为模型中无意识的数据点存在，它们的物理形式早已变成纸浆。 除非法律框架发生变化或公众压力迫使公司保留原件，否则亚历山大图书馆将再次被烧毁。

德里克·麦克阿瑟 (Derek McArthur) 是一位专注于电影和文化的艺术家和艺术作家。 他每周为《先驱报》撰写艺术专栏。
